ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: As shown in the figure, an inclined plane with an inclination angle of 30° is connected to a horizontal plane. On the horizontal plane, a semicircular vertical baffle with radius R is installed. A small ball of mass m is released from rest from a height R/2 on the inclined plane, and when it reaches the horizontal plane, it can just move while sticking to the inner side of the baffle. Neglect the volume of the small ball, friction, and loss of mechanical energy. Then what is the magnitude of the pressure exerted by the small ball on the baffle when it moves along the baffle?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In the figure, on the left is a section of inclined plane marked with an inclination angle of 30°, and the small ball is located on the inclined plane; beside it, a vertical arrow marks the height of the initial position of the small ball relative to the bottom horizontal plane as R/2. The lower end of the inclined plane is connected to the horizontal plane on the right; on the horizontal plane there is a semicircular vertical baffle, and its diameter is marked as 2R in the figure, corresponding to a radius of R. After the small ball reaches the horizontal plane, it makes circular-arc motion along the inner side of the baffle. Then reason: The small ball is released from rest from a height R/2, and friction and loss of mechanical energy are neglected, so from the release point to the horizontal plane, apply conservation of mechanical energy: mg(R/2)=mv^2/2, obtaining v^2=gR. When the small ball moves while sticking to the inner side of the baffle of radius R in the horizontal plane, gravity mg and the supporting force of the horizontal plane balance in the vertical direction and do not provide horizontal centripetal force; the normal force of the baffle on the small ball provides the centripetal force required for circular motion. Therefore N=mv^2/R=m(gR)/R=mg. By Newton's third law, the magnitude of the pressure exerted by the small ball on the baffle is equal to the magnitude of the supporting force exerted by the baffle on the small ball, so the pressure is mg.
